sentence: The kettle still sits where she left it, half-full, the water inside gone stale. I keep meaning to pour it out and never quite do. Her slippers are by the radiator. Her cardigan hangs on the back of the kitchen chair. I sit at the table some evenings and listen to the fridge hum, and the silence has a weight I did not know silence could have. The house does not feel empty exactly. It feels held open, like a door waiting for someone who is not coming back.

I found her glasses on the windowsill last Tuesday. They were folded carefully, the way she always folded them, lenses down on a clean handkerchief. I cannot bring myself to move them. Moving them feels like agreeing to something I have not yet agreed to.

The mail piles up on the hall table. Her name still on most of it. I sort it slowly in the evenings, and each envelope is a small unkindness, the world insisting she should still be opening these things.

The bed still has her shape in it, or I imagine it does. I sleep on my side now, the side I always slept on, and the other half stays cool. I do not know how long the body keeps the memory of another body lying beside it. Long enough, it turns out. Longer than seems fair.

There is a list on the fridge in her handwriting. Bread, milk, the name of a book she meant to order. The magnet is a yellow daisy. I do not take the list down. I do not buy the things on it. It stays there, a small unfinished errand, and I leave the house with it watching me from the kitchen.
Her coat still hangs in the hall. I touch the sleeve sometimes when I come in from the cold, and the wool feels the way it always felt, as if nothing has changed at all.

I made tea for two this morning out of habit and stood at the counter looking at the second cup for a long time. Then I drank one and poured the other down the sink, and the running water sounded too loud in the kitchen, and I had to sit down for a while.

Her plants are dying one by one. I water them when I remember. I forget more than I remember. The fern by the window has gone brown at the edges, and I think she would have known what to do, and I do not, and so it goes.

The clock in the hallway stopped a week after she died and I have not wound it. The hands sit at twenty past three, an arbitrary time, the time of nothing in particular, and yet I look at them every time I pass and feel that some agreement has been quietly broken.
I sleep with the radio on low now. Voices in the next room, even strangers, even the shipping forecast at dawn, are easier than the absence of voices. It is a small thing to admit. I admit it anyway.

The light goes early now and the sky over the rooftops is the colour of wet paper. I stand at the window with the curtain in my hand, not closing it yet, watching the last of the day get smaller. The street is quiet. A car passes. The wind moves something in the gutter. I think about the word evening and how it used to mean dinner and a lamp lit early, and how it means something else now, something I do not have a name for.

The leaves are mostly down. The trees on the road look thinner than they did in summer, and the sky shows through them, a flat grey nothing. I walk the long way home and I do not know why except that the house is quieter than I want to be tonight.
Someone is burning leaves three gardens over. The smoke comes through the open window and I sit with it, not moving, and the smell makes me feel old in a way that is not about age.
I put the lamp on at four. The kitchen takes its evening shape, the long shadows of the chairs, the pool of light on the table where no one is sitting. I make a small dinner I will not finish.

The rain starts somewhere around five and goes on without commitment, a thin steady noise on the roof. I make a list of things I might do and do none of them. The evening passes in the manner evenings have learned to pass without me.

The garden is brown at the edges and the lawn has stopped growing. I look out at it from the kitchen and think how short the days have become, and how the dark seems to come up out of the ground now rather than down out of the sky.
Somewhere a church bell rings the hour and I count without meaning to. Six. The day is gone, then. I sit in the chair by the window and the chair is cold even with me in it.

A blackbird is singing on the fence at dusk. It sings the same three notes over and over, and the song sounds like a question no one has answered, and I stand by the back door listening until the cold reaches my hands.

I close the curtains at half past four. It is too early but the room feels better with the dark shut out, or perhaps shut in. I cannot tell which. I sit with a cup of tea going cold and I am not waiting for anything.

The day ends without much fanfare. The last light leaves the bedroom wall by ten past five. I lie on the bed for a while in my coat, watching the ceiling, and then I get up and put the lamp on and the day is over.

I found a packet of them at the back of the desk, tied with a brown ribbon. The paper was thin and the ink had gone almost violet with age. I sat on the floor and read three before I had to stop. They were full of small kindnesses, things he had noticed about a Tuesday, the colour of a sky, a joke I no longer remembered. I tied them up again and put them back. Some things are not for reading more than once.

Her handwriting was slow and careful, the way she did everything. I held the page up to the light, the way I used to hold her face up to look at her, and there she was again, just for a moment, in the curve of a letter G.

There is a postcard from a place I have never been. The stamp is faded and the message is short and the signature is from someone I never met but my mother loved once, briefly, before my father. I do not know what to do with it. I put it back where I found it.

I read the last letter again and it ends mid-sentence, as if she meant to come back to it and never did. The pen mark trails off after the word and. I sat with that and for a long time before I folded the paper.

The envelopes still smell faintly of her perfume. I do not know how that is possible after so many years. I do not lift them to my face anymore. It is too much, and I am too tired to bear too much these days.

He wrote in pencil and the pencil has gone soft on the page over the years. Some words are barely there at all. I trace them with a finger as if I could press them back into being, and of course I cannot, and of course I keep trying.

There is a letter from a hospital. There is a letter from a friend who has also died. There is a letter from a year I do not want to be back in. I close the drawer and stand in the room and the room does not know what to do with me.

I think about throwing them away and I cannot. I think about reading them all and I cannot. They sit in the drawer and they wait and they will outlive me, probably, and I do not know what becomes of letters with no one left to read them.

I found one I had written and never sent. The address is on the front in my own younger handwriting and the stamp is unposted. I do not remember why I did not send it. I read it and it was a good letter. It made me sadder than the ones I received.
The ribbon is fraying. I keep meaning to replace it. I never do. It is the same ribbon she used, and replacing it feels like losing her hand on the knot.

The lights buzz faintly overhead, the kind of sound you stop hearing and then hear again at three in the morning. The floor is the colour of nothing and the walls are the colour of nothing and a trolley clatters somewhere far off and someone is crying quietly behind a door that does not quite close. I sit on a plastic chair and look at my hands. They are not doing anything. They will not need to do anything for a long time yet.

A nurse walks past and does not look at me. I do not blame her. There is nothing to say and the saying of it would make it worse. The corridor goes on for what feels like miles and the light at the end of it is the same light as the light I am sitting under.

Someone brings me a paper cup of tea. I hold it because it is warm. I do not drink it. The tea goes cold in my hands and I keep holding it because putting it down feels like agreeing to be here for longer.

The clock above the nurses' station says four. I have been here since some other time I cannot remember. Time has gone strange and pale in the hospital light. There is a vending machine humming at the end of the corridor and I find that I am crying without sound.
Through the window in the ward door I can see him in the bed, smaller than he was, the blankets too big around him. He is sleeping. I am glad he is sleeping. I do not go in.

A man with a mop comes down the corridor pushing a bucket on wheels. The water makes a long slow shining trail behind him and he is humming under his breath, a song from a long time ago, and the song is the saddest thing I have heard all night.

A doctor comes to talk to me and she is kind. She uses the careful words they use. I nod in the right places. When she leaves I sit very still and I think how strange it is to have understood every word and yet to feel as if she has been speaking in a language I do not know.
The chairs are bolted to the floor in a row. I have moved between three of them in the night, as if a different chair would make a difference. None of them does. None of them was ever going to.

Outside the window at the end of the corridor the sky is starting to go a little grey. Morning is coming and I am not ready for morning. Morning will mean decisions. Morning will mean the world going on, which is a thing I cannot quite imagine just now.
I close my eyes for a moment and lean my head against the wall. The wall is cool. The wall does not mind. There is some small comfort in the wall not minding.

He said goodbye in the way he says goodbye now, soft and quick, before either of us could think too hard about it. I held the phone for a while after the line had gone dead. The kitchen was very quiet. I could hear the fridge again. I think the kitchen has always been able to hear me but I had forgotten, while he was on the line, that it was listening.

We ran out of things to say about ten minutes in and stayed on the line another twenty anyway, listening to each other breathe across the ocean. When she said she had to go I said yes, of course, and we both pretended I had something to do as well.

There was a delay on the line and so we kept talking over each other and laughing and then not laughing, and then there was the click and the silence and I sat on the end of the bed for a while looking at my own face in the dark window.

He asked about the weather. I told him about the rain. He told me about the heat where he was. We spoke about the weather for a long time and underneath the weather were all the things we were not saying, and the not-saying was louder than the rain.

My mother said love you and rang off before I could answer and I sat with the phone warm in my hand and thought about how she has been saying it like that for years now, as if afraid the line will go before she gets to.
She told me she was tired and going to bed. It was three in the afternoon where I was. The afternoons were going to be long after we hung up. I knew this already. Knowing it did not help.

The call ended and I went outside and stood in the small back garden and the sky was a soft drained blue. I could not remember the colour of the sky where she was. It used to be that I knew that. I do not know when I stopped knowing.

My father's voice was hoarse on the phone and I did not ask why. He said the small things he always says. He said the road was busy yesterday. He said the dog was eating again. He said take care of yourself. He has been saying take care of yourself for forty years and tonight it sounded different.
We said the same goodbye three times. Neither of us wanted to hang up. In the end the line dropped on its own and I think we were both relieved.

After he hung up I scrolled back through old messages from him. They were so ordinary. A photo of a bird on a fence. A grocery list. A two-word reply to something I had forgotten saying. The ordinariness of them was unbearable in a small slow way that took the rest of the evening to live through.

The rain has been steady since lunch. The kind of rain that does not commit to anything, just sets in for the rest of the day. I have washed up. I have read four pages of a book I do not like. I have stood at the window. I have made tea. The afternoon is long and grey and unhelpfully patient, and I am inside it the way a fish is inside water, not noticing it most of the time and then suddenly aware of it everywhere.

Children went past in raincoats earlier, holding their mother's hands, and one of them was crying in a small bored way that was not really crying. The mother kept walking. I watched them out of sight and went on standing at the window for a long time after they were gone.

The radio is on quietly. A man is reading the football scores. The football scores are the same sad sound on a Sunday they were when I was a child, and I do not know whether I am sad because of them now or whether they only sound sad because I am.
The cat has been asleep on the chair since before I woke up. I envy the cat. I sit with my hand on her back and feel her breathing and the small movement is the most alive thing in the house.
The clock has gone slow somehow. I keep checking and only a few minutes have passed. The Sunday afternoon has the texture of a long held breath.

I thought about ringing someone. I went through the names in my head and could not think of anyone who would not be in the middle of their own quiet Sunday, who would want the phone to ring just now. I made another cup of tea instead.

The rain rattles on the conservatory roof in waves. Loud, then softer, then loud again. The wind has picked up somewhere. The branches outside move slowly, the way old people move, and the leaves come off one or two at a time.

I made a Sunday roast for one and ate it slowly and put the rest in the fridge. The kitchen smelled of rosemary and onions. The smell was the smell of a happier time and the kitchen and I could not quite live up to it.

I lay on the sofa after lunch with the rain on the window and tried to read and could not concentrate and put the book on my chest and watched the ceiling for a while. The ceiling has a small damp spot in the corner. I have known about it for years and never done anything about it.

By four it was already starting to feel like evening. The rain had not stopped. I sat in the half-light and did not turn the lamp on for a long time. Some afternoons are like that. You let them be dark.

I drove past the old house yesterday for the first time in years. The new owners have painted it a colour I do not like. The willow at the gate is gone. The porch has been closed in. I sat in the car at the kerb for a while and could not work out if I was looking at my house or at a house that happened to be standing in the same place.

The wallpaper in the upstairs room had small blue flowers. I doubt it is still there. I doubt anything is still there. The house has been sold twice since we left and the people who live there now do not know I exist, and yet some part of me has never quite stopped being eight years old in that bedroom.

The lane is the same. The lane has not been told that anything has changed. I walked it slowly in the morning, and the hedges were the same hedges, and a bird made the same noise from the same tree, and I felt as if I were trespassing on my own life.
The garden gate still sticks the way it did. I do not know why this is the thing that made me cry. I stood with my hand on the latch for some time and then walked back to the car without going in.

The kitchen window used to look out on the apple tree. The apple tree is gone. I think someone has built a shed where it stood. A shed where my mother used to slice apples and call me in for supper. It is a small thing. It is a small absolute thing.

The number on the door is still the same brass number. I noticed that and stood looking at it for a while, and then a man came out of the house and asked if he could help me, and I said no, I was sorry, I had lived there once. He nodded and went back inside. He did not ask anything else. There was nothing to ask.
I drove away slowly. I did not look back in the mirror. I have been there in my head every day for thirty years and the visit had been brief and I was not sure now if I was glad I had gone.

The lilac by the gate is the only thing that is still mine. It blooms every May, the new owners must wonder why, and the smell when I was small was the smell of summer beginning. I cannot smell lilac anywhere now without being briefly small and a long way from here.

There were children in the garden. They were not mine. They were not me. They were doing what children do and they did not see the car, and I watched them for a moment with the kind of love you cannot put down anywhere.
The road home was long and I did not turn the radio on. I drove in the silence and the silence was full of all the rooms I could not walk back into, all the doors that no longer open for me.

sentence: He had a long coat on and the coat was old. I noticed that as he walked away. I had known him through every year of that coat. I cannot now see a coat like it without my chest going slightly tight.

The ground was hard with frost and the gravediggers had been at work since before dawn. The light was thin and the trees were bare and the air smelled of cold earth. We stood in our coats and our breath went up in small white clouds together. The priest said the words. None of us listened too closely. We were each somewhere else, inside the same morning, holding the same small grief in slightly different ways.

His daughter laid a single white flower on the coffin. Her hand was shaking and the flower fell sideways and she had to bend down and right it. No one moved to help. We all watched. It was the most tender thing I have ever seen.

The hymn was one he had liked. We sang it badly in the cold. Our voices came out cracked and our breath went up. The organ played a little behind us, patient with us, and the church was full and no one was looking at anyone else.

After the service the village hall had been laid out with sandwiches and tea. People stood holding plates and not really eating. The room was warm and the windows had steamed up. I watched the steam slide down the glass and felt I had to go outside and stand in the cold to remember where I was.

His widow stood very straight by the door, thanking everyone as they came in. She thanked each of us with the same words. By the end of the morning the words had worn smooth in her mouth like a stone.

The cars left the churchyard one at a time and the snow had begun to fall in small slow flakes. I sat in mine and let the engine warm. Outside, the man in the dark coat was filling in the grave. I could not watch and I could not look away.

We told stories about him in the corner of the hall. Each story was a small return. Each one ended with the small surprise of remembering that he would not be hearing them. We laughed and stopped laughing and laughed again. It was the only way through.

His coat was on a hook in the back of the hall. Someone had brought it in. I do not know who. I do not know why. I stood looking at the coat for a long time and then I left without saying goodbye to anyone.

The church bell rang twice for him as the coffin went out, and the sound went out across the white fields and was very small in the size of the morning. I think that was the moment I understood. I understood it then. I have been understanding it slowly ever since.

Driving home in the dark afterwards the snow had stopped and the road was empty. I did not turn the radio on. The car was warm and the windscreen was clear and the world went past in shapes I did not feel like looking at.

I sent the message late and he had not replied by morning and he had not replied by lunch. I picked the phone up at three. I picked it up at five. By evening I had stopped picking it up so often, and by night I knew. I do not need anyone to say anything. The silence is its own news, and I have been reading it carefully all day.

She read it. The two grey ticks turned blue an hour ago. There has been nothing since. I am surprised by how much the small blue ticks can hurt and how unreasonable it is to be hurt by such a small blue thing.
I drafted a follow-up and did not send it. I drafted another. I deleted them both. I put the phone face down on the table and went into the kitchen and made dinner I could not eat.

I scrolled up through the old conversation and the replies used to come quickly. They came in the middle of sentences, eager, full of typos. I read the old replies and I felt sorry for the person who had written them as if they were not me.
Three days have gone past. I have stopped checking the phone every few minutes. I have started checking it every hour, which is worse, because it means I have learned to wait.

I see her online. I see her not typing. The little ellipsis does not appear. I sit and watch the screen and try to be the kind of person who is not sitting and watching the screen. I am not, just now, that kind of person.

His last reply was two months ago. It was warm and it was long. I had hoped for something that would let me forget those two months. The hope dimmed and dimmed and is now a small thin thing I am embarrassed to keep alive.

I think about deleting the conversation. I do not. Deleting it would be a small admission, and I am not yet ready for the small admission, and so I leave it and it sits there and the unanswered message is at the bottom of it like a stone at the bottom of a pond.

A week now. I sent one more, light and short, an obvious offer of an exit. No reply. I think the silence is the kindest thing he could give me, and I think it is the cruellest thing he could give me, and both are true.

I will stop sending. I will stop hoping. I have promised this to myself before and will probably break the promise again. There is a small private cruelty in being the one who cares more, and I have known about it for a long time, and I am still in the middle of learning it.

It sits on the mantelpiece in a tarnished silver frame. The two of them on the church steps, young, squinting in the spring sun, both their hands full of confetti. They look so certain of each other. They had no way of knowing. I pick it up and dust it sometimes and put it back, and the dust comes back the next week, and I dust it again. It is a small ceremony I do not know how to stop.

Her dress was simple and the photograph is black and white and so the dress is a soft grey and the bouquet is a darker grey. She was so beautiful that morning. He was very nervous. I can see it in his hands. His hands were a little stiff against the side of his suit.

There are people in the background I do not recognise. They must have been there. They must have been someone to them. They are all dead now, all of them, and I am the only one left who knows where the photograph lives.

The bottom corner is creased where someone once held it tight. I do not know who. I think probably her, in some hard year I never knew about. The crease will not come out. The crease is part of the photograph now.

Sometimes I take it down and turn it over and read the date written on the back in pencil. May the eleventh. The pencil mark is faint. I trace it with a finger. I do not know what I am hoping to feel.

I am older now than they were that day. That fact arrived quietly one afternoon a few years ago and has not gone away. I stand in the front room and look at the two of them, young and certain, and they look at me from inside the frame as if they cannot quite see me.

My granddaughter asked who they were last week. I told her. She nodded politely and went back to her game. She has every right to her own afternoon. I sat with the photograph for a while after she left.

I sometimes think I should put it away. Some days the photograph is more than I can bear in the corner of my eye. But the mantelpiece without it would be worse than the photograph with it, and so it stays, and so I dust it on Wednesdays.
The silver of the frame is going dull and I no longer polish it. The dullness suits it now. The photograph is allowed to be old.

I look at her smile in it and I look at her smile in my memory and they are not quite the same smile. The photograph has a smile I no longer trust. The memory has a smile I am not sure I am inventing. Between them there is just the silver frame and the small dust I will wipe again on Wednesday.

We had told no one. There was nothing yet to tell, only what we had told each other in the kitchen at night, in low voices, holding each other's hands across the table. The bleeding started on a Tuesday morning and by Tuesday evening it was over, and we sat on the bed in the half dark and did not speak, and there were no flowers to receive and no one to ring, and only the two of us knew that the small possible thing was now gone.

She stayed in bed for two days. I brought her toast she did not eat. I sat on the chair by the window and read the same page of a book over and over. The room was very quiet. The cat came in and lay across her feet, which was a kindness neither of us could quite manage.

I had bought a small book in the second week. It was about names. It sat in the drawer for a long time after. I could not throw it away and I could not look at it. In the end I put it at the back, behind a stack of bills, and I have not looked since.

The next morning I went into work. People asked how I was, in the way they do. I said fine. I sat at the desk and looked at the screen and could not see the letters. At eleven I went to the toilet and cried for two minutes and washed my face and came back, and no one noticed.

We did not tell each other we were sad. We knew. Saying it would have made it bigger than we were able to hold just then. So we made dinner and we ate and we watched something on the television, and we sat closer than usual on the sofa, and that was how we said it.
The nurse on the phone was kind. She said early miscarriages are common. She said the words gently. They were the right words. They did not help in the way the right words sometimes do not help.

For a long time afterwards I would catch sight of a pregnant woman in the supermarket and have to stop in the aisle and pretend to read a label. I did not begrudge her anything. I just had to wait a moment before I could move again.

We never named what it might have been. There was no it yet. There was only what it would have grown into, which was nothing now, which was a small darkness in our days that we walked around without commenting on.

She got pregnant again the following spring. We did not let ourselves be happy about it for a long time. We held our happiness carefully, with both hands, as if it were a small bird that might choose to fly. The baby came. The baby was fine. The small bird that had not flown the year before stayed with us still, very quietly, in a corner of every glad day.

Years later I told a friend about it for the first time. She said she was so sorry. She said the sentence as if she had been waiting to be given the chance to say it, and I had not known I had been waiting to hear it, and we sat in her kitchen for a while not really drinking the tea.

sentence: The empty side of the bed is the part of the house I have not yet found a way to forgive. I do not blame the bed. I do not blame him. But the bed and I and the smooth sheet have an old quarrel that does not go away in the morning.

I cut the heads off the lilies after they had begun to go brown at the edges and I laid them in a row on the kitchen windowsill to dry. There were twelve of them. I had not counted them before I cut them. The sill is full now. The lilies will dry slowly, and the colour will go, and they will not be lilies any more, but they will not be nothing either. I do not know what they will be. I do not know yet what I will do with them.
I pressed a few rose petals from the wreath in the front of a book. The book was the book she had given me one Christmas. I do not know why I chose that book. It seemed the right book.

The flowers had been beautiful at the service. The flowers had been heavy in the front of the chapel, scenting the whole room. The flowers had gone home with people afterwards. Some had stayed at the graveside. Mine had come home in a bunch wrapped in cellophane, and the cellophane had crackled in the back of the car.

I kept the chrysanthemums in water for as long as I could. They lasted nearly three weeks. I changed the water every other day. The act of changing the water was a small grace each evening. The flowers and I were busy together.

The smell of lilies is the smell of funerals to me now. I had loved lilies before. I do not know that I will buy them again. The association has gone too deep. The smell pulls me straight back to the chapel.

The pollen had stained the white cloth on the table. I had washed it three times. The stain had stayed faint. I had folded it anyway. The cloth is in the drawer, with the faint stain, and I know it is there.

When the flowers had finally to be thrown away I took them out into the garden and put them on the compost heap. I stood and looked at them for a moment. The garden was wet. The compost heap was warm under its lid. I closed the lid carefully.

The dried lily heads on the windowsill have gone a pale brown colour. They are brittle. I touch one with a finger and a small piece comes off. The flowers are not really the flowers any more. They are something the flowers have left behind.

I will keep them. I do not know for how long. The kitchen has room for them. They are a small browning row of remembering on the sill. The sun comes in on them in the afternoon. The sun does not mind that they are dead.

Drying flowers from a funeral is a small private occupation that nobody warns you about. It is the kind of thing you only do once or twice in a life, and the doing of it teaches you something the doing of nothing else could.
